knowledge_point.title: Finding a Scalar Factor in a Linear Combination

question.:question/problem:
![](images/81/816c4ecbfe49321bc6b2bc0d72eb61d6ddd1aeae7e76a275df0975439dde5865.png)

Consider the picture above. Given that $c=a+\lambda b,$ find $\lambda .$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find $\lambda ,$ we want to match the expression

$$
c=a+\lambda b.
$$

We are given that one of the components is $a.$ So, we begin with the vector $a,$ and then find the remaining vector needed to reach the point $C.$

![](images/67/6782f2fa59056afd9022edbaf69c44a991bf12a7ac6a190bea3cc08fc7a4996c.png)

Note that in $△OAC,$ we have:

- $AC=2.5|b|$

- $\overset{\to }{AC}$ and $b$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overset{\to }{AC}=2.5b.$

Additionally,

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =\overset{\to }{OA}+\overset{\to }{AC} \\  & =a+2.5b.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $c=a+\lambda b=a+2.5b.$

Since $a∦b,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $b,$ we get:

$$
\lambda =2.5
$$

c=\lambda a+3b.

We are given that one of the components is $3b.$ So, we first draw the vector $3b$ from the origin. Then we complete the path to the point $C.$

$$

- $PC=\frac{1}{2}|a|$

- $\overset{\to }{PC}$ and $a$ have the same direction

Hence, $\overset{\to }{PC}=\frac{1}{2}a.$

$$

Since $a∦b,$ the linear combination can only be written in one way. Equating the coefficients of $a,$ we get:

$$
\lambda =\frac{1}{2}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The arrows show $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$, and $\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf c$ on a square grid.

![](images/9c/9c8e6ce5ab61cd32d5173d7dc35c715e54ba53fe5113573bedfe37cc4f2d7bcc.png)

Given that $\mathbf c=\mathbf a+\lambda\mathbf b$, find $\lambda$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
One component is $\mathbf a$, so begin with $\overrightarrow{OA}$. The remaining vector is $\overrightarrow{AC}$.

![](images/a1/a13ee372cbfbea706174ae57c0c78e02ae19d4e469300b23d4ee779f6b815a3e.png)

The vector $\mathbf b$ goes up two squares. From $A$ to $C$ we go up six squares, in the same direction. Hence

$$
\overrightarrow{AC}=\frac{6}{2}\mathbf b=3\mathbf b.
$$

By the triangle law,

$$
\mathbf c=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AC}=\mathbf a+3\mathbf b.
$$

The vectors $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are not parallel, so their coefficients are unique. Matching the coefficient of $\mathbf b$ gives $\lambda=3$.

knowledge_point.title: Finding a Scalar Factor in a Linear Combination

question.:question/problem:
The arrows show $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf b$, and $\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf c$ on a square grid.

![](images/e7/e781601d7f485104824be4324946dfb9e7adadc23dac64986a35d438f5428aec.png)

Given that $\mathbf c=\lambda\mathbf a+2\mathbf b$, find $\lambda$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First draw $2\mathbf b$ from $O$, and call its endpoint $P$. Since $\mathbf b$ goes one square left and two squares up, $2\mathbf b$ goes two squares left and four squares up.

![](images/81/817a1572fd17f7924f7c4808f04b273ed0ab8ed852368f0f911b40d9b3458b84.png)

The remaining vector $\overrightarrow{PC}$ goes six squares right. It has the same direction as $\mathbf a$, which goes four squares right. Therefore

$$
\overrightarrow{PC}=\frac{6}{4}\mathbf a=\frac{3}{2}\mathbf a.
$$

Using the path from $O$ through $P$ to $C$,

$$
\mathbf c=\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{PC}=2\mathbf b+\frac{3}{2}\mathbf a.
$$

Since $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are not parallel, matching their unique coefficients with $\mathbf c=\lambda\mathbf a+2\mathbf b$ gives $\lambda=\frac{3}{2}$.

Construct the known component first. The vector $\mathbf a$ goes three squares right and two squares up, so $\frac{3}{2}\mathbf a$ goes $4\frac{1}{2}$ squares right and three squares up. Let $P$ be its endpoint.

![](images/27/27fce7c173b5408cedf468544984f9d779c9b8b608569f530dc0f20e71f1ac06.png)

From $P$ to $C$, the remaining displacement is $1\frac{1}{2}$ squares right and three squares up. Compare this with $\mathbf b$, which goes two squares right and four squares up:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Horizontal scale} &= \frac{\frac{3}{2}}{2}=\frac{3}{4}, \\ \text{Vertical scale} &= \frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Both grid displacements have the same positive scale factor. Thus $\overrightarrow{PC}$ has the same direction as $\mathbf b$ and three quarters of its length:

$$
\overrightarrow{PC}=\frac{3}{4}\mathbf b.
$$

The triangle law now gives

$$
\mathbf c=\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{PC}=\frac{3}{2}\mathbf a+\frac{3}{4}\mathbf b.
$$

Since $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are not parallel, these coefficients are unique. Matching the coefficient of $\mathbf b$ gives $\lambda=\frac{3}{4}$.
